title: The Beach at Concón to the Turbine Hall: the Precarios, the Exile, and the Quipu That Remembers Nothing
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Garden Studio and the Beach at Concón

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; day, month and year agree across en.wikipedia and the MoMA artist biography. The coordinate is the canonical Santiago pin this atlas already carries for Lautaro and Pinochet, not a located address: no source names the clinic, the street or the neighborhood of the birth.
stops.campa: A daughter is born in Santiago on the twenty-second of July, in the city Pedro de Valdivia founded as Santiago del Nuevo Extremo and Lautaro rode against four centuries before. The surname she carries is one of the old Chilean names. Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna wrote the national histories that Bernardo O'Higgins is still read through, and Ramón Subercaseaux Vicuña, father of the painter Pedro Subercaseaux, bore it too. Whether any blood runs between those houses and hers, no document reached here says.
suggested_refs: The civil birth register of Santiago for July 1948, not reached in this pass

stops.name: La Florida, the father's garden studio
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sources give only 'the 1950s' for the childhood at La Florida, defaulted here to mid-decade. The garden studio and the childhood paintings are attested, the year is not.
stops.campa: The family lives at La Florida, on the southern edge of Santiago where the city gives out into the Maipo valley. Her father keeps a studio in the garden. She paints there before anyone teaches her to paint: abstract things made in a shed among fruit trees, by a child with no training and no audience. She is working outdoors, in the weather of a valley, years before any institution gives her a room. The Andes stand along the eastern rim of the sky through this whole childhood, close enough to read the snow line from the door.
suggested_refs: The house and garden studio at La Florida, Maipo valley

stops.name: Concón, the first precario on the sand
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the artist's own site, which dates the first precario to circa 1966; no month or day is recorded anywhere reached.
stops.campa: On the sand at Concón, north of Valparaíso where the Aconcagua river meets the Pacific, she begins gathering what the tide leaves: feathers, sticks, shells, thread, plastic. She builds small assemblages at the waterline and lets the sea take them back. She calls them precarios. They are made to be lost. For a decade none of them is exhibited or sold. Fifty-six years from now the same materials will hang the full height of the Turbine Hall in London; here they are debris arranged where the water will reach it.
stops.quote: The quipu that remembers nothing, an empty cord was my first precario (c. 1966).
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'Quipus' page (ceciliavicuna.com/quipus), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: The tide line at Concón, at the mouth of the Aconcagua

stops.name: Universidad de Chile, the Tribu No
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the enrollment and the daily writing; the March date is the ordinary start of the Chilean academic year and is an inference. The founding of the Tribu No is dated 1967 by en.wikipedia and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: She enrolls at the Universidad de Chile to study architecture and transfers into fine arts. She is writing seven thousand words a day into an experimental book she calls El Diario Estúpido. With others she founds the Tribu No, a collective staging actions in the streets and the countryside around Santiago, refusing on principle to make objects that keep. Salvador Allende is three years from the presidency. In six years she will be out of the country, still working this way.
stops.quote: Tired of my room's normality I have criss-crossed it with a blue thread...taut and geometrical as a sky to communicate with other worlds.
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'Quipus' page (ceciliavicuna.com/quipus), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: El Diario Estúpido, the experimental book of 1966, and the surviving records of the Tribu No

stops.name: Mexico City, El Corno Emplumado prints the first poem
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved. en.wikipedia and Poets.org both give 1967 and are followed here; the research pool's geography lens gave 1966 and es.wikipedia gives 1968. Month and day are recorded nowhere. The coordinate is the city center: the magazine's editorial address is undocumented and this pin is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: The bilingual quarterly El Corno Emplumado, published out of Mexico City, prints her first poem. She is eighteen and has never been to Mexico. The magazine is the hinge of the continental avant-garde in those years, carrying Beat poets and Latin American vanguardists in facing columns, and it drops a Santiago student into a conversation running from New York to Havana to Buenos Aires. Her name is in print among writers she will not meet for decades.
suggested_refs: The 1967 numbers of El Corno Emplumado, Mexico City

stops.name: Universidad de Chile, the MFA
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia; the month of conferral is not recorded and is defaulted.
stops.campa: She takes her Master of Fine Arts from the Universidad de Chile. Allende has been president a year, and the country she graduates into is the one the Unidad Popular is building; she belongs to its artistic left without reservation. She is twenty-three, a poet who makes objects and an artist who writes, and no institution in Chile has yet decided which of the two it is going to call her. Within eighteen months a British Council award will take her to London for a postgraduate year.
suggested_refs: The Facultad de Bellas Artes degree records of the Universidad de Chile, 1971

segments.name: London: the Award and the Coup

stops.name: Slade School of Fine Art, London: the British Council award
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the September date is inferred from the British academic year, since no source records the month of her arrival.
stops.campa: A British Council Award carries her to London for postgraduate study at the Slade School of Fine Art, behind the University College quadrangle in Bloomsbury. She arrives a foreign student with a scholarship and a return ticket, meaning to take a year or two and go back to Santiago. Twelve months separate this arrival from the morning that makes the return impossible. She spends them at the boards and in the libraries; no work she makes in London before the following June is recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The British Council award records for 1972 and the Slade registers

stops.name: London, the four hundred objects for the Chilean resistance
stops.date_confidence: attested with unusual precision: en.wikipedia gives the span as between June 24, 1973 and August 1974. The coordinate is the London city pin; no source names the room the objects were made in.
stops.campa: Between the twenty-fourth of June and the following August she makes over four hundred small assemblages in London: debris, wire, thread, feather, wool, each no larger than a hand. She gathers them under one title, A Journal of Objects for the Chilean Resistance. They are political work disguised as nothing at all, made in a rented room in a foreign city for a country that is about to stop existing in the form she left it in. The Tate will one day hold them in its collection. In 1973 they are rubbish on a table.
stops.quote: Precarious means prayer, uncertain, exposed to hazards, insecure. Prayer is change, the dangerous instant of transmutation.
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'About' page (ceciliavicuna.com/about), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: A Journal of Objects for the Chilean Resistance, Tate collection

stops.name: London, the day the return closes
stops.date_confidence: the coup date is attested to the day; that she was in London on it is attested by en.wikipedia, which states the London exile plainly. The linkage between the coup and her particular decision not to return is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of September the palace of La Moneda burns in Santiago, Salvador Allende dies inside it, and Augusto Pinochet takes the country. She is in London. The return ticket becomes waste paper. The Estadio Nacional fills the next day with detained Chileans, musicians and poets of her own generation among them, and in November the secret police are constituted at a house called Londres 38, an address in Santiago named for the city she is now stranded in. She does not go home for years.
suggested_refs: Londres 38, Santiago, and the Estadio Nacional, both carried in this atlas under Augusto Pinochet

stops.name: Royal College of Art, Kensington: Artists for Democracy
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia; the month of the festival is not recorded in any source reached and is defaulted.
stops.campa: With others she founds Artists for Democracy and helps mount the Arts Festival for Democracy in Chile at the Royal College of Art in Kensington. Exiled Chileans, British sympathizers and artists from other dictatorships hang work in the same rooms and hand the proceeds to the resistance. The group will keep working under that name for years, and its papers will one day be shown in Santiago. She is twenty-six and has been out of her country two years, with no date of return in prospect.
stops.quote: There is a deep human desire for fair relationships, and this need should be the basis of all exchanges.
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'Quipus' page (ceciliavicuna.com/quipus), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: The Artists for Democracy archive, shown at Santiago in 2014

stops.name: Teatro La Candelaria, Bogotá: the second country
stops.date_confidence: the 1975 move from London to Bogotá is attested by en.wikipedia; the month is not recorded. The theatre collaboration is reported without dates by the MoMA biography and is a reconstruction placed at the arrival.
stops.campa: She leaves London for Bogotá, drawn by research into indigenous art, and stays five years. She works on stage designs with Teatro La Candelaria and the Corporación Colombiana de Teatro in the old colonial quarter under the mountain. Colombia is less a second exile than a redirection: she has gone looking, on the continent itself, for the Andean traditions no Chilean art school taught her. The quipu, the knotted Andean cord, is what she is circling in these years, though she does not yet give the work that name.
suggested_refs: Teatro La Candelaria production records, Bogotá, 1975 to 1980

stops.name: Caracas, the research travel through Venezuela and Brazil
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The travel through Venezuela and Brazil is attested only in general terms, with no dates and no named stops; the year and the Caracas coordinate are both anchors chosen to stand for a route that is undocumented.
stops.campa: From the Bogotá base she travels through Venezuela and Brazil, following textile and oral traditions into places no biography records by name. Claude Lévi-Strauss did his own South American fieldwork forty years earlier among the Caduveo, the Bororo and the Nambikwara, Brazilian peoples and not Andean ones, and read their designs as a structure of signs. She is after the other thing, the hand that ties the knot. What she gathers on these roads enters no publication. It comes out later in the fiber work.
suggested_refs: The undocumented Venezuelan and Brazilian itineraries of 1975 to 1980, a stated gap

stops.name: Bogotá, El Vaso de Leche
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia; no month, day, or street location for the action is recorded in any source reached.
stops.campa: Children in Bogotá are dying of contaminated milk. She performs El Vaso de Leche in the street: a glass of milk tied with a red cord, tipped over, spilled onto the paving where anyone passing can watch it run. The action lasts minutes and leaves nothing behind but a stain and the people who saw it. She has been making objects that are witness to a relationship for thirteen years. Here the object is a glass of poisoned milk, and the relationship is a state's toward its own children.
stops.quote: An object is not an object. It is the witness to a relationship.
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'About' page (ceciliavicuna.com/about), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: Photographic documentation of El Vaso de Leche, Bogotá, 1979

stops.name: Bogotá, the film asks the street what poetry is
stops.date_confidence: year attested. The place is a correction: the research pool filed this film under New York, but en.wikipedia states she made it while in Bogotá, Colombia, and it is pinned accordingly.
stops.campa: Still in Bogotá, she makes the film ¿Qué es para Usted la Poesía?, putting the question to people in the street: what is poetry to you. Drivers, vendors, passers-by answer on camera. The film will enter the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The question goes to people who had not been asked it before, and the answers are kept as they were given: the poem is not the poet's property, and it belongs to whoever is asked for it. She leaves Colombia in the same year, northward, for good.
suggested_refs: ¿Qué es para Usted la Poesía?, 1980, Museum of Modern Art collection

stops.name: New York City, the arrival and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and the MoMA biography; the month of the move and the date of the marriage are not recorded in any source reached.
stops.campa: She moves to New York City and marries the Argentine painter César Paternosto. The city becomes her base for the rest of her working life, held against Chile rather than in place of it. She arrives as a Latin American artist into a downtown that has a category for that and very few institutions inside it: the network that shows her for the next decade runs through SoHo lofts and alternative spaces, not through the museums uptown. She is thirty-two and has lived in four countries in eight years.
suggested_refs: The New York lofts and alternative spaces of the early 1980s Latin American circuit

stops.name: Museum of Modern Art, New York: the film enters the collection
stops.date_confidence: the holding is attested but the acquisition year is not: en.wikipedia says only that the 1980 film is now part of the MoMA collection. The stop is dated to the year of the work, and the accession year is a stated gap. The research pool's claim that MoMA exhibited her during the 1980s was not supported by any source and is not carried.
stops.campa: The Museum of Modern Art takes ¿Qué es para Usted la Poesía? into its collection. The film made on the streets of Bogotá now sits in the holdings of the institution that defines, for most of the world, what modern art was. The work itself is changed by nothing in this: it is still a question asked of strangers who had not expected to be asked. What changes is that the question is now kept, catalogued and lent, from a building fifty blocks north of the loft she lives in.
stops.quote: The poem is not speech, not in the earth, not on paper, but in the crossing and union of the three in the place that is not.
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'About' page (ceciliavicuna.com/about), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: The MoMA accession record for ¿Qué es para Usted la Poesía?, year not established

stops.name: Exit Art, New York: Precarious
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The MoMA biography gives the venue, the title and the year; no month is recorded, and the gallery coordinate is approximate to the block.
stops.campa: Exit Art gives her a solo exhibition and calls it Precarious. The objects she made in a London room while her country was being taken now hang in a New York gallery under the name she first gave the form at Concón at eighteen. Seventeen years separate the making from the showing. New York meets the practice at its middle and takes the word precarious for a style, which is not what she has ever meant by it. She means prayer, and exposure, and the dangerous instant in which one thing turns into another.
suggested_refs: Exit Art exhibition records, New York, 1990

stops.name: Villa Serbelloni, Bellagio: the first residency
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The MoMA biography gives the Rockefeller Foundation residency and the year only; the month and the length of stay are not recorded.
stops.campa: The Rockefeller Foundation puts her at the Villa Serbelloni above Bellagio, on the promontory where the two arms of Lake Como divide. It is her first international residency: European institutional comfort extended to a practice built out of tidewrack and thread. She will be brought back to this same villa twelve years on. Between the two stays her work moves out of the alternative spaces of lower Manhattan and into museums, and the objects grow from the size of a hand to the size of a room.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Foundation Bellagio Center residency records, 1991 and 2003

stops.name: University Art Museum, Berkeley: El Ande Futuro
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Venue, title and year come from the MoMA biography; no opening date is recorded and no exhibition catalogue was reached.
stops.campa: El Ande Futuro opens at the University Art Museum in Berkeley. The title says what the work has been arguing since Bogotá: the Andes are not a past to be recovered but a future to be built toward. California receives it as Latin American art. She means it as a proposition about time, and about which direction the continent's oldest technologies are pointing. She is forty-four and has lived outside Chile for twenty years, with Pinochet still commanding the army of the country she was born in.
suggested_refs: El Ande Futuro, University Art Museum Berkeley, 1992

stops.name: New York, the Andy Warhol Foundation Award
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the en.wikipedia awards list, which names QUIPOem as the work honored; no ceremony date or place is recorded, and the coordinate is the city pin.
stops.campa: The Andy Warhol Foundation gives her its award for QUIPOem. The word is her own welding, quipu into poem, and it names the thing she has been building since the beach at Concón: a knotted cord that carries no data and stores no account, made to be a poem standing in space rather than a record standing for something else. The Inca kept their reckonings and their histories in knotted cord, and the Spanish burned them. She ties cords that were never a language, and calls the loss by its name.
stops.quote: My 'quipu' is a poem in space, unlike any 'quipu' that existed before.
stops.quote_source: Cecilia Vicuña, official artist website, 'Quipus' page (ceciliavicuna.com/quipus), English text by the artist
suggested_refs: The Andy Warhol Foundation award citation for QUIPOem, 1997

stops.name: Middletown, Connecticut: the first book of the case
stops.date_confidence: the 1997 date is a resolution, not a fresh finding: the research pool recorded the de Zegher volume as undated, and the year is fixed by the QUIPOem title it shares with the 1997 Warhol award. Publisher records confirm Wesleyan University Press with the Kanaal Art Foundation.
stops.campa: Catherine de Zegher's volume The Precarious: The Art and Poetry of Cecilia Vicuña appears from Wesleyan University Press at Middletown, made together with the Kanaal Art Foundation at Kortrijk in Belgium. It gathers the precarios and the quipus under one curatorial reading and is the first book to argue they are a single practice and not two. It carries the QUIPOem title and shares its year with the Warhol award. Twenty-five years before the Golden Lion, a scholar has already written out the case.
suggested_refs: The Precarious: The Art and Poetry of Cecilia Vicuña / QUIPOem, Wesleyan University Press, 1997

stops.name: Hallwalls, Buffalo: Cloud-Net sets out
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The MoMA biography gives the three-city tour and the year; no opening dates are recorded for any of the three legs.
stops.campa: Cloud-Net opens at the Hallwalls Contemporary Arts Center in Buffalo and begins a year on the road through American alternative spaces: DiverseWorks in Houston next, then Art in General in lower Manhattan. The work is a net, a woven thing hung in the air of a room. It travels the circuit of artist-run spaces rather than the museum circuit, which has not asked. She is fifty. The institutions that will one day build rooms for her fiber work are twenty years out from noticing.
suggested_refs: Cloud-Net tour records: Hallwalls Buffalo, DiverseWorks Houston, Art in General New York, 1998

segments.name: The Anthology and the Archive Returned

stops.name: New York, the Oxford Book of Latin American Poetry
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested by en.wikipedia and the Oxford University Press record; the coordinate is her city of residence, not a located event.
stops.campa: With Ernesto Livon-Grosman she co-edits The Oxford Book of Latin American Poetry: five centuries of verse from the pre-Columbian to the living, in Spanish, Portuguese and indigenous languages, faced with English. The Washington Post is reported to have called it magisterial, though this pass did not reach the review itself. She published her first lines in a Mexico City quarterly at eighteen. At sixty-one she is deciding, from a desk in New York, what the canon of a continent contains.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Book of Latin American Poetry, Oxford University Press, 2009

stops.name: New York, Spit Temple
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested by the Ugly Duckling Presse record; no month recorded, and the coordinate is the publisher's and the artist's city rather than a located event.
stops.campa: Spit Temple: The Selected Performances of Cecilia Vicuña appears from Ugly Duckling Presse, translated and edited by Rosa Alcalá. Her oral work, which existed as breath in rooms and on beaches and was never meant to be fixed anywhere, is set into English on paper. It is the standard bargain of the archive: the thing survives by becoming another thing. She has been arguing with that bargain since the first precario she allowed to be documented rather than surrendered to the tide.
suggested_refs: Spit Temple, Ugly Duckling Presse, 2012, translated and edited by Rosa Alcalá

stops.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, Santiago: the exile archive comes home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The MoMA biography gives the exhibition, both venues and the year; no opening or closing dates were reached.
stops.campa: The Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes in Santiago mounts Artists for Democracy: El archivo de Cecilia Vicuña. The papers, objects and posters of the London group she founded in 1974 come back to the capital as an archive, into a state museum, forty years after they were made against the state that then held the building. She is sixty-six. Chile receives the exile's paperwork nine years before it receives the exile's art; the retrospective in this same building comes in 2023.
stops.quote: Never, never. I come from a family where my mother didn't know she was indigenous because her culture had been demolished.
stops.quote_source: Boston Art Review, interview with Jameson Johnson on 'Disappeared Quipu' at the MFA Boston
suggested_refs: Artists for Democracy: El archivo de Cecilia Vicuña, Santiago, 2014

stops.name: Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago: the precarios as evidence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, concurrent with the Bellas Artes showing. The MoMA biography reports the two venues together without dates.
stops.campa: The same archive shows concurrently at the Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, the museum Chile built to hold the record of the dictatorship: the disappeared, the torture houses, the Estadio Nacional, Londres 38. Her precarios enter that building as evidence, catalogued beside the documents of Pinochet's own apparatus. Objects made of thread and rubbish in a London room in 1973 are filed in Santiago in 2014 as part of the national memory of what was being done in the months she was making them.
stops.quote: We now live in a culture that denies pain and denies trauma, and therefore if you deny that, not only are you bound to repeat it, but you're bound to live in a world of lies.
stops.quote_source: Boston Art Review, interview with Jameson Johnson on 'Disappeared Quipu' at the MFA Boston
suggested_refs: Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos, Santiago, and the Londres 38 site carried in this atlas under Augusto Pinochet

stops.name: Contemporary Arts Center, New Orleans: About To Happen
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the MoMA biography; the opening date within 2017 is not established and is defaulted to the first of January.
stops.campa: About To Happen opens at the Contemporary Arts Center in New Orleans, described as a lament and a love letter to the sea. She is sixty-eight and the work has turned toward drowning coasts and rising water, which is the subject the precarios always had: things at the tide line, made of what the water brought, waiting for the water to come back for them. The city it opens in knows the argument from its own recent water and does not need it explained.
suggested_refs: About To Happen, Contemporary Arts Center New Orleans, 2017, and its subsequent national tour

stops.name: EMST, Athens: documenta 14 opens
stops.date_confidence: attested: documenta 14 ran in Athens from 8 April to 16 July 2017. The coordinate stands roughly four hundred metres east of the EMST building on Kallirrois Avenue and is retained from the research pool rather than silently adjusted.
stops.campa: documenta 14 opens in Athens at the National Museum of Contemporary Art, ahead of its German half. The exhibition that has convened at Kassel every five years since the war gives a second city a co-equal full-scale presentation for the first time, and does it in the capital that Europe's debt machinery had spent the decade disciplining. Her work hangs among the artists documenta has chosen to stand for the moment. Which pieces were shown in Athens and which in Kassel is not recorded in any source reached here.
suggested_refs: The documenta 14 Athens catalogue, not reached in this pass

stops.name: Fridericianum, Kassel: the German half
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Kassel presentation of documenta 14 ran from 10 June to 17 September 2017.
stops.campa: In June the German half opens at the Fridericianum and the other Kassel venues, the exhibition on its home ground in Hesse. She is inside documenta at sixty-eight, which in the arithmetic of European art institutions is late, and which for a Latin American woman working in unspun fiber is ordinary. Five years from now the Venice Biennale will give her a Golden Lion for lifetime achievement. The lifetime in question is fifty-one years old and has run mostly outside rooms like these.
suggested_refs: The Fridericianum and the Kassel venues of documenta 14, 2017

stops.name: Princeton University Art Museum: the Elson residency
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and the MoMA biography; the months of the residency are not recorded and the date is defaulted.
stops.campa: Princeton University Art Museum names her Sarah Lee Elson International Artist-in-Residence and brings her onto the New Jersey campus to research and to make. The residency sits inside a year that also holds three museum exhibitions. She is seventy, and the year's schedule would be called a breakthrough in a younger artist. The practice behind it ran for five decades without institutional support, and the institutions are now arriving all at once, inside the same twelve months.
suggested_refs: Princeton University Art Museum, Sarah Lee Elson International Artist-in-Residence records, 2018

stops.name: Brooklyn Museum: Disappeared Quipu
stops.date_confidence: the venue and year are attested; the day-level run of 18 May to 25 November comes from the MoMA biography alone and is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Disappeared Quipu opens at the Brooklyn Museum and runs from May into November: unspun wool hung the height of the room, cords holding no record, lit and sounded. The title says the double disappearance she works in. The Inca quipus were burned by the Spanish, and the Chileans taken after 1973 were called the disappeared. One vanished writing stands in the room for the other. Neither is being reconstructed here, only shown to be missing, at the scale a museum permits.
stops.quote: First and foremost, I want people to know that the quipu exists.
stops.quote_source: Boston Art Review, interview with Jameson Johnson on 'Disappeared Quipu' at the MFA Boston
suggested_refs: Disappeared Quipu, Brooklyn Museum, 2018

stops.name: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston: the quipu travels
stops.date_confidence: venue and year attested by en.wikipedia; the exact opening and closing days are unverified because mfa.org returned HTTP 403 and 404 in this pass. The research pool's claim text carried the year as 1918, a century off, and has been corrected to 2018.
stops.campa: Disappeared Quipu travels to the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, opening in October 2018 and closing in January 2019. The museum keeps an Andean textile holding of its own, so the new cords hang in the building that already stores the old ones behind glass. What she is after is not the artifact under the vitrine but the thing the artifact was made for, and she says plainly, to an interviewer that autumn, that what she wants first is for people to know the quipu exists at all.
stops.quote: It is the spirit of the quipu that excites me. The quipu works because it is simultaneously here and not here.
stops.quote_source: Boston Art Review, interview with Jameson Johnson on 'Disappeared Quipu' at the MFA Boston
suggested_refs: Disappeared Quipu, Museum of Fine Arts Boston, October 2018 to January 2019

stops.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Philadelphia: the first American survey
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the MoMA biography; no opening date within 2019 was reached and the date is defaulted.
stops.campa: The Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania gives her the first major solo museum exhibition of her career in the United States. She is seventy-one and has lived in New York since 1980, showing in alternative spaces and university galleries for four decades. The American museum system reaches her in Philadelphia in 2019, fifty-three years after the first precario went into the water at Concón and twenty-nine years after Exit Art showed the same objects downtown.
suggested_refs: The ICA Philadelphia exhibition of 2019, her first major United States solo museum show

stops.name: Madrid, the Premio Velázquez
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and the Spanish Ministry of Culture record. The Madrid coordinate is the prize's administrative seat, not a confirmed place of receipt: no ceremony date or venue was established in this pass.
stops.campa: Spain awards her the Premio Velázquez de Artes Plásticas, administered from Madrid by the Ministry of Culture, in the same year the Herb Alpert Award for Visual Art reaches her from California. The kingdom whose functionaries burned the knotted cords of the Andes honors the artist who ties them empty and hangs them in rooms. Where the ceremonies were held and on what days is not established in anything reachable, and the pin here marks an office rather than an occasion.
suggested_refs: Premio Velázquez de Artes Plásticas award file, Spanish Ministry of Culture, 2019
sources: Spanish Ministry of Culture award record

segments.name: The Golden Lion and the Turbine Hall

stops.name: Giardini della Biennale, Venice: the Golden Lion
stops.date_confidence: the award and the year are attested by the Venice Biennale record; the date of the ceremony was not confirmed in this pass and April is the month the 59th Biennale opened. The day is not asserted.
stops.campa: At the fifty-ninth Venice Biennale she is given the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, shared that year with Katharina Fritsch. These gardens have honored this kind of career at this kind of distance before. Arthur Bispo do Rosário, who sewed his blue thread for decades inside a Rio asylum and made a mantle to be judged in, was brought to the Giardini in 1995, six years dead. She is alive, seventy-three, and in Venice to take it in her hands. Two of the largest rooms in the world are already booked for her that same year.

This time it is the art and not the paperwork. Fifty-one years after a British Council award took her out of the country for what everyone understood to be a postgraduate year, the national museum of Chile hands her its rooms, and the title on the wall tells the country to dream the water. She is seventy-four. The Andes she read the snow line of from a garden door in La Florida stand east of the building.

The country that could not be returned to in 1973, whose government would have arrested her, whose secret police were constituted at Londres 38 that November, names her its laureate at seventy-five. She takes it as the daughter of a family in which, as she has said elsewhere, her own mother did not know she was indigenous, because the culture had been demolished before she was born to be taught it.

Victoria Ocampo built Sur here to make Latin American letters into one conversation; Leo Chiachio and Daniel Giannone stitch their own cosmologies in embroidery a few neighborhoods off. stops.campa: Quipu Gut opens at the Pérez Art Museum Miami, on the bay, in the American city that speaks most of the languages of her continent. The knotted cords have been given a body here: gut, the interior rope, the coil that digests what is taken in. She is seventy-six. Quipu Womb, Disappeared Quipu, Quipu Gut: one word carried a decade through different rooms and different organs, and the cords in each of them still hold no record of anything. Fifty-eight years separate this bay from the tide line at Concón, and the materials have not changed.
